answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (i.e. a Cosmos DB account).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. (No extra extension required.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-01' = { name: 'myAccount' ... kind: 'MongoDB' }). Terraform (AzRM provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" resource_group_name = "myRg" location = "West US 2" offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use a MongoDB-style URI. Typical form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. SRV form may be offered: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Port for direct TLS connections: 10255. Required options commonly: ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false (Cosmos Mongo API historically requires disabling retryWrites), and appName or maxIdleTimeMS as desired.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed in Cosmos DB terms using Request Units (RU/s). For MongoDB API you provision RU/s at account/database/collection level (or use autoscale RU). Cosmos also exposes serverless and autoscale options in some SKUs; there is also a newer vCore/dedicated offering for certain managed MongoDB products but the common billing model to expect is RU/s (provisioned or autoscale) or serverless where available.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary auth for the MongoDB API is username/password (the account database user credentials/key material exposed by Cosmos). For other Cosmos APIs there are primary/master keys and Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) integration for management operations. For a MongoDB driver to use Azure AD you'd need an authentication flow supported by the MongoDB protocol (Cosmos historically expects username/password), so in practice applications use the MongoDB username/password (or the account name + primary key), or the standard MongoDB SCRAM credentials exposed by Cosmos. If you require Azure AD bearer-token auth for data-plane MongoDB connections, that is not the default path; you would instead use Azure AD for management plane (az login / RBAC) and keep driver auth as username/password. (If you plan to use AAD for the MongoDB API, plan for additional gateway/preview features — low confidence.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. mongodb npm driver, and Mongoose on top of it). There is no separate MongoDB-specific SDK for Cosmos DB; you speak the MongoDB wire protocol, so use normal MongoDB tooling/drivers. For management tasks use az CLI/ARM/Bicep/Terraform or Azure SDKs (Microsoft.Azure.Cosmos) for the SQL API, but for data access in this sample use mongoose/mongodb.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Historically Cosmos DB did not expose native MongoDB-style vector index creation; newer vector-capable offerings reference algorithms such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. If the cluster supports vector indexes the likely Mongo-style createIndex call looks like: db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vectorOptions: { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine', efConstruction: 200 } }). (This is an example form; exact option names vary by preview/implementation.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) for full‑text and hybrid (text+vector) search integrated with Cosmos DB (indexers or data pipelines). The MongoDB API does not expose an independent full‑text engine with the same feature set as Azure Cognitive Search. For hybrid relevance (text + vectors) you generally index documents in Azure Cognitive Search and combine vector scoring with text scoring there or at application side.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API implements a range of MongoDB wire protocol versions and exposes compatibility levels (historically 3.2 → 3.6 → 4.0 → 4.2 → 4.4 → 5.0, and more recent accounts may support 6.x/7.x). Check the account's "server version"/API compatibility in the portal. Common unsupported or partially supported features historically include some server-side JavaScript (mapReduce/$where), certain aggregation stages/operators, and some admin commands; also wire-protocol edge cases and extensions may not behave exactly like upstream MongoDB. Expect subtle differences and test your workloads. (Pick the account-level MongoDB compatibility to match your driver version.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development (Microsoft's emulator image mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator for Linux Docker or the Windows installer). The emulator's HTTPS endpoint is typically on 8081; for MongoDB protocol testing the emulator can expose Mongo endpoints but behaviour varies—many teams instead run a real MongoDB Docker image locally (mongo:6) on the default MongoDB port 27017 to develop the app logic and then verify against the live Cosmos account. If you must test against Cosmos semantics, test against the real Azure account rather than assuming perfect parity with a local Mongo container.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB provides a native change feed for the SQL/Core API. For the MongoDB API, change streams (the watch() API) are supported on accounts that expose the corresponding MongoDB server version/feature level. No separate portal toggle is usually required beyond using a MongoDB-compatible account that advertises change stream support. Ensure the account compatibility/server version supports change streams and that you use an appropriate driver version.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The service-specific MCP server for this sample is the documentdb MCP server (i.e. the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data‑plane tooling for Cosmos DB / MongoDB API). The general azure MCP server does not substitute for the documentdb-specific tools used to inspect collections/indexes/query plans for a Cosmos DB account.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally launched a service called DocumentDB which later evolved and was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB exposes multiple APIs including the original DocumentDB (SQL) API and a MongoDB-compatible API. This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is not the same as any separate open-source "DocumentDB" project — the names overlap historically but Cosmos DB is Microsoft's managed, proprietary multi-model database service implementing multiple APIs.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB uses Microsoft’s proprietary distributed storage/engine and implements a MongoDB wire-protocol translator for the MongoDB API; it is not running upstream mongod. In practice application code that uses standard MongoDB drivers and standard CRUD/aggregation operations will mostly work, but some server features/commands and behaviors differ (indexes, certain aggregation stages, transactions semantics, latency characteristics), so you must test and possibly adapt queries and indexes for Cosmos semantics.

answers.question: What exact connection URI will the sample read at runtime and where is it stored?
answers.answer: Read the MongoDB-style URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI (do not hard-code); example value pattern to expect: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@

answers.question: Which database name and collections will the sample use and create?
answers.answer: Use database name sample_fintech_07. Collections: transactions (stores ledger postings), exchange_rates (stores rate documents), idempotency (or unique index on transactions.idempotency_key) — create transactions and exchange_rates in sample_fintech_07 and ensure an index on transactions.idempotencyKey (unique) and an index on exchange_rates.currency + date.

answers.question: What exact Mongoose connection options should be used to connect to Cosmos's Mongo API right now?
answers.answer: Call mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, ssl: true, replicaSet: 'globaldb', retryWrites: false, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 30000 }); (Pass these options when starting the app. Use the URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI.)

answers.question: How will the sample implement idempotency and what index is required?
answers.answer: Store an idempotencyKey field on each transaction document and enforce uniqueness via a unique index: db.transactions.createIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 }, { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { idempotencyKey: { $exists: true } } }). On incoming POSTs, attempt an insert with that key inside a transaction or catch duplicate-key errors (E11000) to return 409/ignore duplicate.

answers.question: How will the sample perform multi-document transactions with Mongoose against the cluster?
answers.answer: Use MongoDB transactions via sessions: const session = await mongoose.startSession(); await session.withTransaction(async () => { await TransactionModel.create([ ... ], { session }); await ExchangeRateModel.updateOne(..., { session }); }, { readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' }, writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } }); Ensure the account compatibility supports transactions and use the same database for involved collections. Pass { session } on each operation.
